paper_title: HSPR: Recovering Software-Agent Benchmark Scores via Hierarchical Posterior Inference

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Evaluating software agents on a full benchmark is expensive. A small task subset can preserve agent rankings while yielding inaccurate scores. Historical responses provide useful structure, but tasks with identical source responses can have different outcomes for a new target agent. We introduce Hierarchical Score Posterior Recovery (HSPR), which combines source-fitted response factors with uncertain group success rates. Observed target outcomes update the posteriors over the target latent state and group rates; posterior-guided acquisition selects subsequent tasks. Its score-based criterion equals the expected one-step reduction in full-score posterior variance. Observed successes and posterior-predictive counts for unqueried tasks yield a full-score posterior. The final estimate uses its median with source-selected calibration. At a 10% task budget on four task banks from the SWE-bench family, HSPR achieves the lowest mean absolute error (MAE) on three banks and the lowest maximum absolute error (MaxErr) on all four among the methods compared. Removing group uncertainty or replacing adaptive queries increases macro MAE in the respective controls. Macro MAE decreases across 5-20% budgets.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Evaluating software agent requires repository exploration, code editing, tool use, and execution across hundreds or thousands of tasks (Jimenez et al., 2024; Duan et al., 2026). small execution budget makes this evaluation more practical and creates an inference problem: recovering the agents score on the full benchmark from few observed task outcomes. Accurate score recovery is essential for comparing progress and assessing capability. *Corresponding author. 1 Figure 1: Task-efficient software-agent evaluation. Representative strategies estimate full-benchmark scores from limited target executions. HSPR combines hierarchical response modeling with adaptive querying. The displayed median is the decision before source-selected calibration. At 10% budget on SWE-bench Pro, Mid-Range selection (Ndzomga, 2026) preserves model ordering well (τb = .967), yet its raw subset mean has mean absolute error (MAE) of 22.798 percentage points (pp)  (Table 1)  . Using the same Mid-Range outcomes, source-fitted Ridge estimator reduces MAE to 3.434 pp. Estimation accuracy also varies across task banks: ATLAS-port has MAE of 0.957 pp on Full and 7.736 pp on Pro. Low-budget evaluation depends on both task selection and the estimator applied to the observed outcomes. The source-response signature of task records its binary outcomes across historical agents. Tasks with identical signatures may have different outcomes for new target agent, while still sharing response tendency. Modeling this tendency as an uncertain group success rate lets one observation inform other group members without fixing their outcomes. We ask: How can we recover target agents full-benchmark score from few executions while accounting for uncertainty in how source response patterns transfer to the target? We introduce Hierarchical Score Posterior Recovery (HSPR), illustrated in Figure 1. HSPR uses source-fitted response factors to model target latent response state and uncertain success rates within source-signature groups. Each observed outcome updates the latent-state posterior and the group-rate posteriors. Posterior-guided acquisition selects the next task using these dependencies. Observed successes and posterior-predictive counts for unqueried tasks yield distribution over the full-benchmark score. Its median minimizes modelconditional expected absolute loss; source-only validation selects calibration for the final estimate. At 10% task budget, HSPR achieves the lowest MAE point estimates on Lite, Full, and Pro and the lowest MaxErr on all four SWE-bench task banks compared with the baselines in Table 1. On Verified, its MAE is within 0.055 pp of ATLASport. In the respective controls, removing group uncertainty increases macro MAE, as does replacing adaptive queries with the estimator held fixed. Across 520% task budgets, equal-bank macro MAE decreases as more outcomes are observed. Our contributions are threefold: We introduce HSPR, hierarchical full-score model that combines source-fitted response factors with uncertain target success rates within source-signature groups. We derive posterior-guided acquisition for score recovery, including criterion equal to the expected one-step reduction in finite-score variance. Source-only validation selects the deployed acquisition objective before target evaluation. We provide controlled empirical study across four SWE-bench task banks, including end-to-end hierarchy controls, estimation and acquisition ablations, paired statistical analysis, mechanism diagnostics, and 520% budget sweeps.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Efficient benchmark prediction. Active Testing combines informative queries with sampling correction (Kossen et al., 2021); Active Surrogate Estimators learn surrogate for unobserved errors (Kossen et al., 2022). Random-Sampling-Learn (RSL) uses random-core regression; learned benchmark predictors can fail under extrapolation (Zhang et al., 2025). tinyBenchmarks uses compact calibrated subsets (Maia Polo et al., 2024), while SparseEval optimizes anchors and weights from the response matrix (Zhang et al., 2026). Factorized Active Querying (FAQ) combines historical factors with adaptive querying and finite-population inference (Wu et al., 2026). HSPR uses modelconditional finite-score posterior with global factors and uncertain group rates. Psychometric evaluation. Item-response models calibrate NLP test items (Lalor et al., 2016). Amortized model-based evaluation predicts item difficulty from question content to support adaptive testing (Truong et al., 2025). Agent Psychometrics models task-level agent responses (Ge et al., 2026). ATLAS uses item-response models with Fisher-guided acquisition (Li et al., 2026); PTAIRT uses historical trajectory information for task selection and reconstruction (Duan et al., 2026). HSPR builds on historical item calibration but adds residual response dimensions and conditional target-specific group rates. ATLASs Fisher-guided acquisition targets latent ability. HSPRs scorevariance criterion targets the full-benchmark score, accounting for dependence among unobserved outcomes. Subsets and objectives. Historical pass-rate selection can preserve software-agent rankings (Ndzomga, 2026); subset quality depends on task banks and representations (Gusev and Zaytsev, 2026). SubLIME predicts subset-to-full rank correlation from anchor models and dataset characteristics (Saranathan et al., 2025). Ranking measures relative ordering (Liu et al., 2025), while score recovery requires an accurate numerical scale. Agent evaluation context. HELM, BIG-bench, MMLU, and Dynabench cover heterogeneous evaluation settings (Liang et al., 2023; Srivastava et al., 2023; Hendrycks et al., 2021; Kiela et al., 2021). AgentBench and AgentBoard evaluate tool use and multi-turn agents (Liu et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2024). EarlyEval reduces within-task execution through early outcome prediction (Shi et al., 2026). Trajectory-based selection (Ayyad et al., 2026) and process-aware adaptive testing (van der Linden, 2008) use additional observations. HSPR uses source binary responses and observed target outcomes.

sections.content: 4.1 Experimental Setup We evaluate held-out agent configurations on four archived task banks from the SWE-bench family. Fulls 2,294 tasks form approximately 276 source-signature groups on average across targets, giving N/ = 8.32  (Table 3)  . An observed outcome updates the posterior over the shared group success rate, informing predictions for unqueried group members. Baselines retain their saved budget-specific settings. 4.6 Discussion Conditional on the target latent state, the second term in Equation 12 scales with the number of other unqueried group members and the posterior variance of their common rate. At fixed taskbank size and rate posterior, an observation can inform more remaining outcomes in larger group. Fulls larger source-signature groups  (Table 3)  permit more within-group sharing than Verifieds, consistent with its larger hierarchical gain  (Table 2)  . As queries reveal outcomes, the remaining group sizes and rate posteriors change, altering this contribution to Score acquisition.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: HSPR combines source-fitted response factors, uncertain group success rates, and posterior-guided acquisition to estimate full-benchmark scores from limited observations. Its final estimate uses posterior median with source-selected calibration. At 10% task budget, HSPR achieves the lowest MAE point estimates on three of four SWE-bench task banks and the lowest MaxErr on all four among the compared methods. Controlled experiments show substantial aggregate gains from adaptive querying. The contribution of group uncertainty varies across task banks, with the largest observed improvement on SWE-bench Full. These results highlight the role of historical response structure in task-efficient score recovery.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: We evaluate held-out agent configurations on four task banks from the SWE-bench family. Generalization under substantial shifts in model families or agent scaffolds remains to be evaluated. HSPRs response factors and source-signature groups are derived from the historical source bank and therefore depend on its coverage. Posterior uncertainty is conditional on the assumed response model, including within-group exchangeability. We measure evaluation budgets by the number of distinct target-task executions and report evaluator inference overhead in Appendix G. Token, wall-clock, and monetary savings depend on pertask execution costs and cannot be inferred directly from task-count reduction. Historical data collection, source fitting, and configuration selection incur additional costs.

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.content: This study uses existing software-agent response matrices and does not involve human participants or private user data. Treating recovered scores as fully observed results may mislead model comparisons, particularly when historical source data poorly represent target configuration. We therefore recommend reporting the evaluation budget and clearly distinguishing recovered scores from full-benchmark measurements.

sections.title: Reproducibility
sections.content: Algorithm 1 operates on fixed task bank and reveals target outcomes through its execution oracle. During source validation, the entire held-out row is removed before fitting initialization rates, item parameters, residual factors, and source signatures. The model is then refitted on all source rows using the selected configuration. All model, query-policy, and calibration choices are frozen before target replay. At each step, acquisition uses sources and observed history only. Exhausted groups are excluded, and one remaining task is sampled uniformly within the selected group before revealing its binary outcome. Every path contains distinct executions. Each method and query path has its own B-execution budget. Predictive draws use numerical generator separate from query selection. The score estimate and queried task identities are recorded before full target outcomes are accessed. Full truth then supplies MAE, ranking, and maximum error. The complete target folds are pooled within each query seed before metrics are averaged, as defined in Section 4.1. This ordering separates inference information from scoring information. Historical bank collection and source fitting are additional costs outside B. Adapted baseline protocols. FAQ-port uses the without-replacement variant and caps its logistic factor rank at the source cohort size minus one. It retains posterior factor updates and the PAI estimator; this variant does not inherit the withreplacement coverage theorem. ATLAS-port retains sequential expected-a-posteriori ability estimation, maximum-Fisher-information selection with top-five randomization, and p-IRT score estimation. It uses the source-fold 4PL bank in place of the original R/mirt 3PL fitting and applies fixed distinct-task budgets. Thus these rows report adapted procedures on the available banks. RSL uses the Uniform query set; Mid-Range raw and Mid-Range with Ridge share their source-selected task set. Neither shares HSPRs adaptive query paths. PTA-IRT retains its released frozen predictions, including its use of historical trajectory information. The matched target-task budget does not equalize historical information or source-fitting costs.

sections.title: H Score Recovery Across Model Families
sections.content: Figure 4 compares full-benchmark scores with HSPR estimates at the 10% task budget. Each point represents one target configuration, with model families distinguished by color and marker. The diagonal shows exact agreement, making overestimation and underestimation visible across the score range. The relative errors of the represented families vary across task banks. On Lite, GPT/o-series configurations have lower mean error than Claude configurations (1.71 versus 2.15 pp), while the ordering reverses on Verified (1.70 versus 1.52 pp). Full shows consistently small errors across its configurations: the GPT/o-series, Claude, and unspecified groups have mean errors of 0.39, 0.80, and 0.74 pp, respectively, and every configurations mean absolute error is below 1.71 pp. The individual points also reveal variation among configurations within family that is hidden by family averages. sections.title: G Computational Overhead
sections.content: We profiled HSPR at the 10% task budget over all 133 target configurations and five query seeds (665 runs). Experiments used an AMD EPYC 7352 server with 96 logical CPUs and approximately 566 GiB of system memory, running Python 3.11.3, NumPy 1.26.4, and SciPy 1.17.1. We ran 24 evaluations concurrently, each in separate process with one CPU thread, without GPU. Timing includes posterior initialization, sequential querying and updates, and the final predictive decision and calibration. It excludes data loading, source fitting and configuration selection, and software-agent task execution. Table 8 reports per-run wall times on shared server. The complete batch took 510.1 seconds with concurrent evaluation; the timed inference intervals consumed 3.31 CPU hours in total.
